\title{When the Light Goes Out: Silent and Visible Failure\\of SLAM on a Ground Robot}

\begin{abstract}
% No citations, symbols, maths or footnotes.
A robot that knows it is lost can stop; one that trusts a wrong pose keeps driving. We therefore ask whether the failure of a localisation and mapping system is visible when the light is switched off. Two monocular systems built on 3D foundation models, VGGT-Long and MASt3R-SLAM, and \todo{the systems of the other members} run on three indoor sequences of a public ground-robot dataset with motion-capture ground truth and a LiDAR reference map. In normal light VGGT-Long has the lower trajectory error. When the light switches on and off, it still reports a pose for every frame and no error, yet its trajectory is no better than that of a robot that never moves. MASt3R-SLAM reports itself lost for most of the dark time and, on the same timestamps, has half the error. The underlying model marks dark images with its lowest possible confidence, but nothing marks the wrong trajectory that follows. Code and results are public at github.com/eliasbitsch/bEARL.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Service robots move through rooms where lights are switched on and off. A camera-based system is expected to degrade in the dark; what matters for safety is whether it notices. Failure detection is an open problem of robust simultaneous localisation and mapping (SLAM)~\cite{cadena2016past}, and learned trackers tend to replace explicit tracking loss by silent drift~\cite{thomas2026failure}. 3D foundation models, now built into SLAM systems~\cite{deng2026vggtlong,murai2025mast3rslam}, have not been tested this way. On a real light on/off sequence we ask: \emph{(RQ1)} how accurate are trajectory and map in normal light, \emph{(RQ2)} how does each system fail in the dark, and \emph{(RQ3)} does the system itself report the failure? Light is the stress test, not the finding. We contribute an evaluation under real illumination change with motion-capture ground truth, a documented silent failure with a test of its cause, and an open pipeline.

\section{State of the Art}
DUSt3R regresses dense point maps for image pairs~\cite{wang2024dust3r}; VGGT takes many images and outputs camera poses, depth and point maps in one forward pass, without bundle adjustment~\cite{wang2025vggt}. VGGT-Long joins overlapping chunks of VGGT predictions with similarity transforms (Sim(3), i.e.\ rotation, translation and scale) estimated on the shared frames and closes loops in a Sim(3) pose graph~\cite{deng2026vggtlong}. MASt3R-SLAM tracks frames against keyframes with MASt3R matches, optimises a keyframe graph with loop closure and relocalises when tracking fails~\cite{murai2025mast3rslam}.
\stixSota\ \zhouSota\ \ovdiienkoSota

Robustness is often tested with synthetic perturbations, but a synthetic illumination change can reverse the ranking that real adverse conditions produce~\cite{thomas2026failure}. Under synthetic low light, MASt3R was rated robust by tracking success and trajectory error~\cite{kumar2026uavslam}, without asking whether a failure would be noticed. Introspective perception predicts the failures of vision systems~\cite{rabiee2020ivslam}. VGGT's per-pixel confidence is trained as aleatoric uncertainty~\cite{wang2025vggt,kendall2017uncertainties}; VGGT reports no pose uncertainty, and its confidence predicts pose failures only partly~\cite{srinivasan2026vggtknow}. 3D foundation models produce consistent-looking geometry even for uninformative input such as noise~\cite{paul2026onescene}.

\section{Materials and Methods}
\textbf{Dataset.} M3DGR~\cite{zhang2025m3dgr} is recorded with a wheeled robot carrying an RGB-D camera (RealSense D435i, $640\times480$, 30\,Hz), a Livox MID-360 LiDAR, IMUs and wheel odometry; ground truth comes from motion capture at about 300\,Hz. We use three sequences in one $6.5\times3$\,m room: \emph{Dynamic01} (D; 175\,s, 71\,m, people walking), \emph{Sha-turn01} (S; 139\,s, 98\,m, sharp turns) and \emph{Varying-illu01} (V; 154\,s, 72\,m, light off five times for 12 to 16\,s; 46\,\% of its frames have more than 80\,\% of their pixels below grey value 20 of 255).

\textbf{Systems.} Both systems use the authors' default parameters on the RGB images and ran on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU. VGGT-Long (chunks of 60 frames, overlap 30, loop closure) gets every third frame (10\,Hz), as its authors advise for dense input; MASt3R-SLAM gets all frames and exports keyframes only. \stixMethods\ \zhouMethods\ \ovdiienkoMethods

\textbf{Metrics.} The absolute trajectory error (ATE) is the root mean square (RMS) of the position error~\cite{sturm2012benchmark}, computed with evo~\cite{grupp2017evo} on poses matched within 10\,ms after Umeyama alignment~\cite{umeyama1991least}, Sim(3) for monocular systems~\cite{zhang2018tutorial}; we report the median over five runs. Maps are compared with a pseudo-ground truth built by stacking MID-360 scans along the motion-capture poses, with the marker-to-LiDAR offset chosen to make the cloud as sharp as possible~\cite{levinson2010unsupervised}; after trajectory alignment and iterative closest point (ICP) refinement we report the F-score at 10\,cm~\cite{knapitsch2017tanks} in the volume seen by both maps. For RQ3 we use the correct rate of OpenLORIS-Scene~\cite{shi2020openloris}: the share of the sequence time covered by a correct pose (position error $\le$ 1\,m, orientation error $\le 30^\circ$, each pose valid for at most 1\,s, the values suggested there for room-size scenes); the constant body-to-camera rotation is estimated once on D. A failure counts as visible if the system reports it itself in its log or by relocalising; for VGGT-Long we also write out the mean depth confidence per frame without changing the algorithm.

\textbf{RQ1, accuracy.} In normal light both systems follow the ground truth (Fig.~\ref{fig:traj}). VGGT-Long has a 1.6 to 2.3 times lower ATE than MASt3R-SLAM (Tab.~\ref{tab:results}), also on the same timestamps, but a lower ATE does not imply a better map: on S MASt3R-SLAM's map scores higher. Five runs agree within 0.1\,mm, so their spread says nothing about robustness; only MASt3R-SLAM on V ends at 0.63 or 0.69\,m, as its relocalisation runs in a separate thread.

\textbf{RQ2, failure mode.} VGGT-Long outputs a pose for every frame and ends at 2.35\,m ATE, no better than a robot that never moves (2.39\,m, RMS distance to the ground-truth centroid) and in the range of the visual systems that M3DGR reports for V (TartanVO 2.17\,m, DM-VIO 2.27\,m, VINS-Mono 2.70\,m; ORB-SLAM2 and ORB-SLAM3 fail~\cite{zhang2025m3dgr}). Dark chunks are still joined to their neighbours, the chunk scale collapses step by step and the trajectory shrinks towards the room centre (Fig.~\ref{fig:timeline}). The error is larger in lit frames (2.48\,m) than in dark ones (2.17\,m), so the whole trajectory is wrong. Removing the dark frames from the input does not help (2.34\,m): across each gap the robot moves several metres, and the chunks on both sides hardly overlap. MASt3R-SLAM stops adding keyframes in the dark and, from the second dark phase on, relocalises without success; it is silent during the first one. On its 73 keyframes its ATE is 0.69\,m, VGGT-Long's on the same timestamps 1.50\,m; no keyframe follows after 132\,s.

\textbf{RQ3, detectability.} On V, VGGT-Long covers the whole sequence with poses but has a correct rate of 0.00 (median orientation error $134^\circ$), and it reports nothing. MASt3R-SLAM's correct rate drops from 0.53 and 0.69 to 0.10, and its log shows relocalisation attempts in 43\,\% of the seconds of V and in none of D and S, close to the 46\,\% dark frames; its keyframe-only output also lowers its correct rate on D and S. VGGT's confidence has a median of 4.6 in lit frames and sits at its floor of 1.00 in dark ones (95th percentile 1.16), so the model flags the dark input. In lit frames after the blackouts it is back at 4.6, as on D (5.1), while the pose is 2.5\,m off: nothing flags the wrong trajectory.

As a check, FAST-LIO2~\cite{xu2022fastlio2} (LiDAR and IMU) reproduces the published value on D (0.14 vs.\ 0.13\,m~\cite{zhang2025m3dgr}) and reaches 0.14\,m on V, so scene and ground truth are sound. With half-length chunks (16\,GB GPU) VGGT-Long fails on V alike (2.23\,m), so the failure does not hinge on the chunk length.

\section{Discussion}
High aleatoric uncertainty is the expected answer to a noise-dominated image~\cite{kendall2017uncertainties}, and VGGT gives it. What the per-pixel confidence does not express is the uncertainty of the relative Sim(3) between two chunks, which is what VGGT-Long chains; this matches the finding that VGGT's confidence predicts pose failures only partly~\cite{srinivasan2026vggtknow}. VGGT-Long drops only points below 10\,\% of the lower of the two chunk medians, a relative threshold that two dark chunks pass, so links are fitted to geometry produced from uninformative input~\cite{paul2026onescene}. That this is not the whole cause shows the run without dark frames: it fails alike, because VGGT-Long has no check whether two chunks actually overlap and joins them regardless. Discarding bad input therefore does not fix the failure; it has to be reported or bridged. MASt3R-SLAM switches to relocalisation when the fraction of valid matches falls below a threshold, which turns most of the darkness into an explicit state, but not all of it. This mirrors the split between explicit failure and silent drift of other learned trackers~\cite{thomas2026failure} and is consistent with tracking success hiding a failure~\cite{kumar2026uavslam}. An absolute confidence check per chunk, as used for filtering~\cite{hillemann2026vggtuncertainty}, could at least report the dark input; bridging the gaps with wheel odometry or an IMU is future work.

\textbf{Limitations.} One dataset, room and light-change sequence with five blackouts give a documented case, not a general law. MASt3R-SLAM is scored on keyframes only, which excludes its lost periods; we therefore also compare on common timestamps. The offset between motion-capture body and camera is not compensated, as in M3DGR, and adds a pose-dependent error.

\textbf{Conclusion.} In normal light VGGT-Long is the more accurate foundation-model system (RQ1). In the dark it fails silently and globally, whereas MASt3R-SLAM mostly reports its loss (RQ2). The model's confidence marks dark input, but neither system flags a wrong trajectory once the light is back (RQ3).
